Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT A. Francisco Oold Condominium II, EDSA cor. Mapagmahal St., Diliman, Quezon City OFFICE OF 24 mLG OPINION NO. 10 March 2005 HON. ZURIEL S. ZARAGOZA Sangguniang Panlalawigan Member Provincial Capitol Building Vigan City, Ilocos Sur Dear SP Member Zaragoza: This refers to your request for legal opinion on certain issues relative to the measures passed, sessions conducted and acts of sanggunian members, of your sanggunian, which apparently, as can be deduced from your letter, are perceived by you as either defective or illegal, such that your queries were to the effect of asking the Department on whether the sessions, measures passed and acts of some of your colleagues, are legal/legaJly binding. Please be inforrned at the outset that this Depaftment's duty is to implement the Local Qovemment Code via, inter alia, the rendition of legal opinions. Legal opinions for that matter are executive constructions given by the government agency concemed on a pa#icular law it is tasked to implement. However, legal opinions have its limitations, such that it cannot be rendered on issues that require factual adjudication in view of some conflicting claims. May it be noted that the passage of an ordinance involves two (2) aspects, i.e. (1) the substantive; and (2) the procedural. The former refers to the necessity of an ordinance to comply with the provisions of the Local Qovemment Code of 1991 (RA 7160), other existing laws and the Constitution. The latter, in the meantime, refers to the manner by which an ordinance has to be enacted. Any violation of these two (2) aspects may render an ordinance invalid. As regards the substantive aspect, the same involves a question of law which may be validly addressed through the rendition of a legal opinion, as the latter entails only an interpretation of the provisions of the ordinance visa-vis the laws and Constitution whereupon said ordinance should be compliant with. Insofar as the procedural aspect is concerned, let it be stressed that this aspect usually involves more of questions of fact, because it involves the contemporaneous events that surrounded the procedure/manner of the passage of the ordinance. Sometimes, a necessity of factual determination as to the proper procedure undertaken in the passage of a particular ordinance would become imperative if the matter is

-2- timely raised by any proper party. In such a case, the aid of the court to resolve the issue has to be implored since this Department, not being a court, is not empowered to aqjudicate factual issues. Moreover, please be informed of the rule that measures already passed by the local legislative body enjoys the presumption of validity, which presupposes that the acts of the members of the sanggunian and the sessions conducted that led to the passage of the measures also enjoys the presumption of regularity and validity. Such conclusion is anchored on Rule 131, Section 3 (m) of the Rules on Evidence, Rules of Court, whereby the presumption that official duty has been regularly performed are satisfactory if uncontradicted by other evidence. The "evidence" being referred to now necessitates the production of documentary and testimonial pieces of evidence, before the proper forum, and that is indubitably, our regular courts. Ergo, it is short of saying that your concerns should have been expressed in a proper legal procedure as may be provided for by the Rules of Coun to be filed before the proper court, and not through a letter query before this Department. Be that as it may, for academic discussion, it is wise to advise you of certain points in connection with your queries which are heretofore restated, 1. "There were no Internal Rules of Procedure that was adopted to govem the conduct of the session. Attach (sic) herewith are the minutes the session for July 14 and 20, 2004 which shotvs that the body failed to adopt an IRP in spite of the fact that one member did move for the adoption of the old IRP but was not acted upon by the presiding officer. The presiding officer only manifested in session that the body will maintain status quo, but also failed to present it to the floor for approval. Is there such thing as status quo with regards to the Internal Rules of Procedure? Are the sessions conducted under such set-up legally binding? 2. The pennanent presiding officer, in the person of Vice- Governor Deogracias Victor B. Sa.vellano was absent during the first two sessions, reason by which Board Member Ronald Singson acted as temporary presiding officer on July 14 session and Board Member Jeremias Singson acting as the temporary presiding officer on July 20. It is clearly stipulated in Section 49 of the Local Government Code and Section IO Rule II of the old IRP that in the absence of the presiding officer, "the members present and constituting a quorum shall elect (sic) among themselves a temporary presiding officer".

-3- The minutes of the sessions hereto attached will reflect the absence of an election conducted by the members to choose a temporany presiding officer. In what authority then did Board Member Ronald Singson and Board Member Jeremias Singson got the right to act as temporary presiding officer on those sessions? Are the sessions presided upon by unauthorized temporary or acting presiding officers legal? 3. The provincial board of [locos Sur also failed to elect the chairmen and members of the different standing committees. The presiding officer declared that we should maintain "status quo" with regards to the composition of the committees. This was put into motion and was not approved by the body in session. Several measures had been passed and committee reports were delivered during the two sessions under this set-up. My reservation lies in the fact that we now have a different composition in the provincial board. Some chairmen of some very important committees are now out of the provincial board, how can we then maintain the so-called "status quo"? Are the measures that were approved during those two sessions legally binding? 4. There are measures that were passed without going through committee hearings, 1st nor 2nd readings, only one final reading for according to them it was the standard procedure in the Sangguniang Pantalawigan. Are these measures legally binding? 5. In passing urgent measures, for example, appropriating funds for the Clean and Green program of the provincial government, there are instances where the measures are passed with ncy-c€ff.ification of urgency from the governor or vice governor, and there is no suspension of rules, but it is approved without going through the legal legislative procedures. This is a clear violation of Section 48 Rule VIII of the old IRP. Is this measure legally binding?" Queries 1, 2, 3 and 5 shall be given an omnibus reply. Thus: The Intemal Rules of Procedure (IRP) of the local legislative bodies, ust like the IRPs of both Houses of Congress, are merely designed for the orderly and convenient conduct of the proceedings in the sanggunian. In the case of "Alberto Romulo vs. Nicanor Yniguez" (04 February 1986), the Supreme Court held that "internal rules do not have the force of law but are merely in the nature of by-law's prescribed for the orderly and convenient conduct of proceedings. They are merely procedural rules, not substantive". Thus, for merely being procedural, said "rules adopted by deliberative bodies are subject to revocation, modificatim or waiver at the

-4- pleasure of the body ado tin them "

-5- presiding officer, might be challenged, we cannot lose sight that said temporary presiding officer's authority during that particular session was not challenged, or even if challenged, was acquiesced to by majority of the members present. Such principle now equally applies to your challenge to both the composition of your sanggunian's standing committees and the lack of certification of urgency from the govemor anent the Clean and Qreen program. Moreover, the Committee Report made during the previous set of the sanggunian is also binding insofar as the new sanggunian is concerned, unless reprobated by the latter. Said Committee Report can be considered and/or adopted by the new sanggunian where the chairmanship of committees are, in the meantime, insignificant as what is subject of consideration is the report itself, which can be sponsored by any member pending organization of the different committees. "Anu member" could refer to any new member or a re-elected member, whether or not member of a particular committee concerned. In reply to your fourth query, please be infonned that the Code (RA 7160) is silent on the number of readings that need to be undertaken by the sanggunian before a measure is enacted and sent to the Local Chief Executive for approval. However, the Implementing Rules and Regulations of RA 7160 may shed some light into this matter. Article 107, paragraphs (d) and (f), of the Implementing Rules and Regulations respectively provides: "(d) No ordinance or resolution shall be considered on second reading in any regular meeting unless it has been reported out by the proper commiitee to which it was referred or certified as urgent by the local chief executive. (f) The secretary to the sanggunian of the province, city or municipality shall prepare copies of the proposed ordinance or resolution in the form it was passed on second reading, and shall distribute to each sanggunian member a copy thereof, except that a measure certified by the local chief executive concerned as urgent may be submitted for final voting immediately after debate or amendment during the second reading. xxx. ' Insofar as resolutions are concemed, attention is invited to paragraph (c) of the same IRR which reads: "A resolution shall be enacted in the same manner preschbed for an ordinance, except that it need not go through a third reading for its final consideration unless decided otherwise by a majority of all the sanggunian members'. It may not be amiss to point out that "rules and regulations issued by executive or administrative officers pursuant to, and as authorized by, law have the force and effect of laws" (Warren Manufacturing Workers Union vs. Bureau of Labor Relations, 159 SCRA 387 (1988)).

6- Such being the case, the Implementing Kules and Regulations of RA 7160 requires ordinances to undergo the three-reading rule at least before its enactment while resolutions need not go through a third reading for its passage, unless otherwise decided by a mAjority of all the sanggunian members. As to whether or not the three-reading requirement must be made on separate days or on one day only, the Code and its Implementing Rules and Regulations are silent, thus, the need to examine your IRP. If the latter is also silent on the matter, judicial decisions can be resorted to for guidance. Prescinding from the above, Section 45 of your 2001 IRP reveals that ordinances and resolutions must undergo three readings, albeit, did not likewise state whether three readings shall be made on separate days. Thus, please be informed that in the Resolution dated 28 January 2000 of the Supreme Court En Banc, on the Motion for Reconsideration filed by the Solicitor General on the earlier ruling of the Court in the Malonzo vs. Zarnora case (infra), the Court pronounced that: "There is nothing in the law, however, which prohibits that the three readings of a proposed ordinance be held in just one session day" (323 SCRA 875). Hence, the court ruled that, unlike Congress, the three readings in the sanggunian of a proposed measure can be done in one session since the law does not require that it be done on separate days. Qiven this Supreme Court ruling, the "at least three-reading rule" as required in your IRP may be conducted even in one session day. We hope that we have enlightened you on the matter. Legal: 87 A-a Director Manuel V. DILQ Region 01 San Fernando City, Very truly yours, ANGELO T. REYES Secretary LOCAL PLS SILG05-005315 Biason La Union
